messages.subject_clean: Divergence in results produced by makeADFun in RTMB and the glmmTMB package
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I encountered a problem where I have different estimates and standard errors produced by makeADFun in RTMB and nlminb and by the glmmTMB package. The divergence in the estimated variance of the random effects was quite substantial for the hurdle model in my simulation. My R code for simulation is attached here. If someone could let me know whether I did something wrong or point something to help me understand why that would be the case, I would really appreciate it.

Many thanks,
Jiachen

messages.body_plain:
The main issue is with how you set up your Z matrix, which doesn't
match what glmmTMB does.  See attached (modified) file. Basically, I set up

id2 <- rep(1:20, each = 50)
Z <- model.matrix(~0 + factor(id2))

(and made u0, u1 length-20 rather than length-19).

for n observations and k group, Z is an nxk matrix, not an (n-1)xk matrix.

   Once I do this, the results match quite well.

   For what it's worth, you might be able to use
glmmTMB::dtruncated_poisson() in your likelihood function rather than
writing it out yourself ...

   cheers
    Ben Bolker

messages.subject: monitor memory requirements?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, folks,

   I have a memory-intensive TMB-based calculation. I want to run
experiments scaling the size of the problem to estimate how much memory
I will need in order to do my actual problem of interest.

   I thought that the peakRAM package (which runs R's gc() and records
the results to get an estimate of total and peak RAM used during the
execution of a specified expression) would be useful, but as far as I
can tell it doesn't capture memory used by TMB.

   In particular, I am running a series of experiments where peakRAM
reports at most a few 100 Mb used, but my R session is crashing when my
machine (with 60G of RAM) runs out of memory.

  So I'm looking for a different way to do this, ideally within R, but I
guess I could also try to run an external script to watch the memory
used and match it up with recorded timestamps from my R session ...

   Does anyone have suggestions?

   Ben Bolker

messages.subject: Re: monitor memory requirements?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

This is something we've also run into and I've tried a couple of approaches. For an external script I've had success using something like [memusg script](https://gist.github.com/netj/526585) I've also ran several profiles with valgrind massif and got very similar results to the memusg script linked. That is the most reliable way we have found.

I did also write a small package for doing profiling from R which works for TMB https://github.com/mrc-ide/memprof

If your R session is crashing you can write out the profile to a file and read it in a new session.

>From first session
memprof::with_monitor(my_func(), monitor_file = "myprofile")

In a new session
profile <- memprof::monitor_read("myprofile")
plot(profile)

This will monitor the current R process and any spawned processes meaning the TMB fit should be captured too. `profile` is a data frame of memory usage over time, you can read the max `utils::format.object_size(max(profile$rss), "auto")`

Note that I don't think the profiles from `memprof` are as reliable as memusg/massif in all cases, I've seen weird results when trying to profile anything which knits an R Markdown document but with TMB it has had comparable results.

[jointprof](https://github.com/r-prof/jointprof) also looks really promising for some more detailed output but I haven't tried this in anger. I'd be interested if you have any success with this.

Rob

messages.body_plain:
I asked around and Matthew Supernaw suggested the following:
use Valgrind and lldb or gdb.
valgrind will detect any memory leaks and lldb will catch the source of the crash.

Valgrind:
valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all --track-origins=yes --verbose  --log-file=valgrind-out.txt R -f myscript.R

LLDB:
R -d lldb
run -f myscript.R

I note that Matthew works on a linux machine, though a Windows equivalent of Valgrind is available called Deleaker (see this blog post https://www.deleaker.com/blog/2020/01/04/valgrind-for-windows/).

Best,
Kelli

For the record, I couldn't get memusg to work properly for my application - I was trying to loop over multiple processes and spawn batch jobs (by calling "./memusg Rscript MY_SCRIPT PARAMS" either via system() in R, or from a loop in a bash shell), and things were wonky [presumably because of something about how subprocesses are counted that I don't understand]. However, the memprof package worked perfectly; I looped over problem sizes, saving the cumulative output to a checkpoint file as I went along, so that by the time the script stopped because I maxed out memory at 60G and the R session crashed, I had a nice table of the memory requirements for a range of smaller problems. I ran a log-log regression to estimate the scaling, and think that I have the answer to my question (I'll need about 600G and 3 hours to run my actual problem -- the local HPC cluster has a few nodes this big, hopefully I won't have to wait too long to get access to them).

  cheers
   Ben Bolker

messages.subject: Issues with complex numbers
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to basically run multiple regressions in parallel inside my likelihood function where each one might have a different design matrix. In this case, all 6 design matrices are just an intercept column but the 6. entry has an actual design matrix. I am wondering what might be the tidiest way to organize parameters, as I have 6 parameter vector of different lengths.

I came up with creating a list of design matrices and corresponding parameter vectors inside the likelihood, and just evaluating the linear predictors in a loop. But my first implementation led to weird behaviour, producing complex-valued results.

I compiled a minimal example and would appreciate insights.

Thanks :)

library(RTMB)

# some design matrix
Z = cbind(1, matrix(runif(300), 100, 3))

# parameter list
par <- list(
  eta = rep(-2, 5), # intercepts for the 6 simple regressions
  beta0 = -2, # intercept for regression 4
  beta_z = rep(0, 3) # slopes for regression 4
)

# data list
dat <- list(Z = Z)

# this part below would be inside the likelihood
getAll(par, dat, warn = FALSE)
"[<-" <- ADoverload("[<-") # not sure if this would be needed

# creating a parameter list
beta <- vector("list", 6)
beta[-4] <- eta # scalar entries
beta[[4]] <- c(beta0, beta_z) # vector entry
# list of design matrices
Z_list <- vector("list", 6)
Z_list[-4] <- rep(list(matrix(1, nrow(Z), 1)), 5) # intercept columns
Z_list[[4]] <- Z # proper design-matrix entry

K <- length(beta)

# probably not elegant but fine
nObs <- max(sapply(Z_list, function(z){
  if(is.null(dim(z))){
    return(length(z))
  } else{
    nrow(z)
  }
}))

# to simulate what happens in MakeADFun() turn beta into advectors
beta <- lapply(beta, advector)

# works fine
Eta1 <- matrix(NaN, nObs, 0)
for(k in seq_len(K)) Eta1 = cbind(Eta1, Z_list[[k]] %*% beta[[k]])

# produces matrix with complex-valued entries
Eta2 <- matrix(NaN, nObs, K)
for(k in seq_len(K)) Eta2[,k] = as.numeric(Z_list[[k]] %*% beta[[k]])

head(Eta1)
head(Eta2)

messages.body_plain:
To avoid method dispatch issues, I think it's best to dynamically convert base R objects (e.g. Eta1 and Eta2) using the AD function - see my modified example. You can then avoid the ADoverload hack.
In addition the line

beta[-4] <- eta # scalar entries

seems to behave differently for base R evaluation versus RTMB.
It seems base R automatically converts RHS to a list, so we can help RTMB a bit by changing to:
beta[-4] <- as.list(eta) # scalar entries

Modified example:

func <- function(par) {

    getAll(par, dat, warn = FALSE)

    ## creating a parameter list

    beta <- vector("list", 6)

    beta[-4] <- as.list(eta) # scalar entries

    beta[[4]] <- c(beta0, beta_z) # vector entry

    ## list of design matrices

    Z_list <- vector("list", 6)
    Z_list[-4] <- rep(list(matrix(1, nrow(Z), 1)), 5) # intercept columns
    Z_list[[4]] <- Z # proper design-matrix entry

    K <- length(beta)

    ## probably not elegant but fine

    nObs <- max(sapply(Z_list, function(z){
        if(is.null(dim(z))){
            return(length(z))
        } else{
            nrow(z)
        }
    }))

    ## works fine
    Eta1 <- AD(matrix(NaN, nObs, 0))

    for(k in seq_len(K)) Eta1 = cbind(Eta1, Z_list[[k]] %*% beta[[k]])

    ## produces matrix with complex-valued entries
    Eta2 <- AD(matrix(NaN, nObs, K))

    for(k in seq_len(K)) Eta2[,k] = as.numeric(Z_list[[k]] %*% beta[[k]])

    print(head(Eta1))
    print(head(Eta2))
    return (0)
}

obj <- MakeADFun(func, par)

messages.body_plain:
Without more info - at the very least a 'traceback()' - I can't say for sure, but here is a guess of what might be going wrong:

At some point sdreport calculates the derivative of all ADREPORTed quantities (2808 in your case) wrt all random effects (nr=156*nspace ?) and performs sparse solve using this derivative as RHS.
Because R uses the 32 bit CHOLMOD routines, it can't do sparse solve with RHS longer than ca 2^31.
So, if the number of spatial grid cells for your application is greater that 2^31 / 2808 / 156 = 4902 you might have this problem.
